question:
Given your task update

T_i=Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i),

the top-r SVD components can be obtained efficiently from the smaller projected matrix

B_i=Q_i^\top(W+R_i).

Compute

B_i=\widehat U_i\Sigma_iV_i^\top.

Then

T_i=(Q_i\widehat U_i)\Sigma_iV_i^\top.

Define

U_i=Q_i\widehat U_i.

The rank-r truncated SVD is therefore

T_i^{(r)}
=
U_i^{(r)}S_i^{(r)}V_i^{(r)\top},

where U_i^{(r)}, S_i^{(r)}, and V_i^{(r)} correspond to the r largest singular values.

Concatenating components from all tasks

For N tasks, we concatenates the retained components:

U=
\left[
U_1^{(r)}
\mid
U_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
U_N^{(r)}
\right]
\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times Nr},

V=
\left[
V_1^{(r)}
\mid
V_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
V_N^{(r)}
\right]
\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times Nr},

and constructs the block-diagonal singular-value matrix

S=
\operatorname{diag}
\left(
S_1^{(r)},S_2^{(r)},\ldots,S_N^{(r)}
\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^{Nr\times Nr}.

Before whitening, the direct concatenated reconstruction would be

T_{\text{concat}}=USV^\top.

However, although each U_i^{(r)} and V_i^{(r)} is orthonormal within its own task, the concatenated matrices generally do not satisfy

U^\top U=I,
\qquad
V^\top V=I.

For example, components from tasks i and j may overlap:

U_i^{(r)\top}U_j^{(r)}\neq 0,
\qquad
V_i^{(r)\top}V_j^{(r)}\neq 0.

This cross-task non-orthogonality is the conflict that whitening attempts to reduce.

Whitening the concatenated subspaces

S²MoE performs an SVD of each concatenated basis:

U=P_UD_UQ_U^\top,

V=P_VD_VQ_V^\top.

It then removes the singular-value scaling and constructs orthonormalized matrices:

U^\perp=P_UQ_U^\top,
\qquad
V^\perp=P_VQ_V^\top.

These are the polar factors of U and V. Assuming full column rank, they can equivalently be written as

U^\perp=U(U^\top U)^{-1/2},

V^\perp=V(V^\top V)^{-1/2}.

They satisfy

U^{\perp\top}U^\perp=I,
\qquad
V^{\perp\top}V^\perp=I.

The final merged task update is

\boxed{
T_{\text{merged}}
=
U^\perp S V^{\perp\top}
}

and the shared model weight becomes

\boxed{
\Theta_s
=
\Theta_{\mathrm{pre}}
+
T_{\text{merged}}.
}

This is the shared-module construction described in S²MoE.  

Substituting your projected task updates

Since

U_i^{(r)}
=
Q_i\widehat U_i^{(r)},

the concatenated left matrix is

U=
\left[
Q_1\widehat U_1^{(r)}
\mid
Q_2\widehat U_2^{(r)}
\mid
\cdots
\mid
Q_N\widehat U_N^{(r)}
\right].

Thus, in your setting,

T_{\text{merged}}
=
\operatorname{Polar}
\left(
[Q_1\widehat U_1^{(r)}|\cdots|Q_N\widehat U_N^{(r)}]
\right)
S
\operatorname{Polar}
\left(
[V_1^{(r)}|\cdots|V_N^{(r)}]
\right)^\top.

A key detail is that whitening is applied after concatenating all task subspaces, not independently to each task. Each task’s SVD vectors are already orthonormal internally; whitening is needed primarily to resolve overlap across different tasks.

Also, after whitening,

U^\perp S V^{\perp\top}

is generally not equal to the simple sum

\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i^{(r)}.

Whitening changes the singular directions to produce jointly orthogonal left and right bases while retaining the collected singular-value matrix S.

To construct the sparse experts in S²MoE, start from each fine-tuned model and subtract the shared model.

Let

\Theta_i

be the parameters of the model fine-tuned on task i, and let

\Theta_s
=
\Theta_{\text{pre}}+T_{\text{merged}}

be the shared model constructed from the merged low-rank components.

Then the residual expert for task i is

E_i=\Theta_i-\Theta_s.

This residual contains the task-specific information that is not already represented by the shared model.

1. Express the residual expert

Since

\Theta_i=\Theta_{\text{pre}}+T_i,

we have

E_i
=
\Theta_i-\Theta_s
=
T_i-T_{\text{merged}}.

For your projected task update,

T_i=Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i),

the expert residual becomes

\boxed{
E_i
=
Q_iQ_i^\top(W+R_i)-T_{\text{merged}}
}

for each layer or weight matrix.

This is the dense expert before pruning.

2. Apply magnitude pruning

Suppose a layer residual is

E_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.

Flatten it into a vector:

e_i=\operatorname{vec}(E_i).

Choose a retention ratio \rho\in[0,1]. If the layer has mn entries, retain

k=\lfloor \rho mn\rfloor

entries with the largest absolute values.

Define the index set

\mathcal I_i
=
\operatorname{TopKIndices}
\left(
|e_i|,k
\right).

The sparse expert is

\tilde e_{i,j}
=
\begin{cases}
e_{i,j}, & j\in\mathcal I_i,\\
0, & j\notin\mathcal I_i.
\end{cases}

After reshaping,

\boxed{
\tilde E_i
=
\operatorname{reshape}(\tilde e_i,m,n)
}

is the sparse expert for that layer.

Equivalently, using a binary mask M_i,

M_{i,j}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & |E_{i,j}|\text{ is among the top }k,\\
0, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}

so that

\boxed{
\tilde E_i=M_i\odot E_i.
}

Here, \odot denotes elementwise multiplication.

3. Why top-magnitude pruning is used

The sparse approximation solves

\min_{\|\tilde E_i\|_0\leq k}
\|E_i-\tilde E_i\|_F^2.

Under a strict k-nonzero constraint, the optimal solution is to keep the k entries with the largest magnitudes.

Indeed, pruning an entry E_{i,j} contributes

E_{i,j}^2

to the reconstruction error. Therefore, the error is minimized by pruning the smallest-magnitude entries and retaining the largest ones.

This is exactly the sparse-expert construction used in the paper.  

4. Layer-wise construction

For a Transformer model, repeat the procedure for every prunable matrix:

E_i^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_i^{(\ell)}
-
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}.

Then prune each matrix independently:

\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}
=
\operatorname{TopMagnitudePrune}
\left(
E_i^{(\ell)},\rho
\right).

The complete sparse expert is

\tilde\theta_i
=
\left\{
\tilde E_i^{(1)},
\tilde E_i^{(2)},
\ldots,
\tilde E_i^{(L)}
\right\}.

Typically, these can include attention projection matrices and feed-forward matrices. Biases, normalization parameters, or embeddings may be left unpruned depending on the implementation.

5. Final S²MoE layer computation

At inference, the shared output is

y_s^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.

The router selects sparse experts and computes

y_{\text{expert}}^{(\ell)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.

The final layer output is

\boxed{
y^{(\ell)}
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}
+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}x^{(\ell)}.
}

Thus, the effective weight for an input is

\Theta_{\text{effective}}^{(\ell)}(x)
=
\Theta_s^{(\ell)}
+
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\tilde\alpha_i^{(\ell)}
\tilde E_i^{(\ell)}.

Compact construction

For each task i,

\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
E_i
&=
\Theta_i-\Theta_s,\\
M_i
&=
\operatorname{TopKMask}(|E_i|,k),\\
\tilde E_i
&=
M_i\odot E_i.
\end{aligned}
}

One notation warning: in the paper, the sparsity parameter is sometimes described ambiguously. A “retention ratio of 0.2” means keeping 20% of the parameters and pruning 80%. Always state clearly whether \rho denotes the retained fraction or the pruned fraction.

slides.title: From Base Weights to Updates
slides.caption: Wₜ = W₀ + Δₜ, for t = 1, 2
slides.narration: Each task starts from the same pretrained layer and adds its own update. We store those updates rather than duplicating the full weight matrix.

slides.title: Two Illustrative Tasks
slides.caption: \Delta_1=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad \Delta_2=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: Task 1 changes the first coordinate direction, while Task 2 changes the second. The tiny matrices make the later subspace operations easy to see.

slides.title: Keep the Dominant Mode
slides.caption: Δₜ is approximately Δₜ(r) = Uₜ(r) × Sₜ(r) × Vₜ(r)ᵀ, with r = 1
slides.narration: We retain only the largest singular mode of each task update. This rank-one approximation is the first compression step.

slides.title: The Two Rank-One Components
slides.caption: Δ₁ = 2 × [1; 0] × [1 0], and Δ₂ = 3 × [0; 1] × [0 1]
slides.narration: In this illustrative example, both updates are already rank one. Their left and right singular directions align with separate coordinate axes.

slides.title: Vectorize the Components
slides.caption: qₜ,₁ = vectorize(Uₜ(r) × Sₜ(r) × Vₜ(r)ᵀ), and qₜ,₁ has 4 entries
slides.narration: Vectorization places every retained component in the same four-dimensional parameter space, so task components can be compared directly.

slides.title: Concatenate Across Tasks
slides.caption: Q = [q₁,₁ | q₂,₁], a 4 by 2 matrix
slides.narration: The two task columns enter one combined matrix before whitening. This preserves the cross-task geometry for the joint operation.

slides.title: Measure Cross-Task Geometry
slides.caption: G = transpose(Q) × Q
slides.narration: The Gram matrix records each component's scale on the diagonal and their inner products off the diagonal.

slides.title: Polar-Factor Whitening

stages: Z = Q × inverse square root of G

slides.caption: Z = Q × inverse square root of (transpose(Q) × Q)
slides.narration: We multiply the concatenated components by the inverse square root of their Gram matrix. This jointly rescales and decorrelates the task directions.

slides.title: Verify Orthonormality

rows: z₁ and z₂ each have length 1

slides.caption: The transpose of Z multiplied by Z equals the identity matrix
slides.narration: Whitening succeeds when the columns have unit norm and zero mutual inner product. They now form a stable shared coordinate system.

slides.title: Project into Shared Coordinates
slides.caption: cₜ = transpose(Z) × vectorize(Δₜ), and the reconstructed update is Z × cₜ
slides.narration: Each task update is projected into the shared whitened basis. Its coefficients are c_t, and Zc_t reconstructs the retained projection.

slides.title: Build the Shared Module
slides.caption: The shared coordinate is a weighted average, and the shared update is reshape(Z × average coordinate)
slides.narration: We average the task coordinates with nonnegative weights summing to one. Reshaping the result produces one shared update.

slides.title: Subtract the Shared Part
slides.caption: Rₜ = Δₜ − shared update
slides.narration: Subtracting the same shared module from each update leaves the task-specific residuals. These residuals are the inputs to expert sparsification.

slides.title: Prune by Magnitude
slides.caption: Keep the largest-magnitude entries. With a 50 percent retention ratio, 2 of 4 entries survive.
slides.narration: The pruning operator keeps the largest residual magnitudes and zeros the rest. With rho equal to one half, two of four entries survive; rho is the retained fraction.

slides.title: Assemble a Compressed Expert
slides.caption: compressed task model = W₀ + shared update + Eₜ
slides.narration: A compressed task model combines the pretrained layer, the persistent shared module, and one sparse task expert.

slides.title: Route at Inference
slides.caption: W(x) = W₀ + shared update + g₁(x)E₁ + g₂(x)E₂
slides.narration: At inference, the router assigns input-dependent weights to the sparse experts. The shared module is always active, while the experts are mixed according to the router.

slides.title: FINAL ANSWER

stages: Q → inverse square root of transpose(Q) × Q → Z
Δₜ − shared update → magnitude pruning → Eₜ
W(x) = W₀ + shared update + sum of gₜ(x)Eₜ

slides.caption: W(x) = W₀ + shared update + sum of gₜ(x)Eₜ; shared update = reshape(Z × average coordinate); Eₜ = prune(Δₜ − shared update); Z = Q × inverse square root of (transpose(Q) × Q)
slides.narration: Rank-one task components are concatenated and jointly whitened to form Z. Their aggregated coordinates create the shared module, pruned residuals create sparse experts, and routing combines everything with the pretrained layer.
